lessons.title: Broiler and layer production basics
lessons.html:
Broiler and layer production basics

The broiler cycle

  1. House preparation: the house is cleaned, disinfected and rested; fresh litter (wood shavings) is spread; feeders and drinkers are set at chick height; heaters are switched on to warm the house before chicks arrive.
  2. Placement: day-old chicks are delivered from the hatchery, counted, checked and placed near feed and water.
  3. Brooding: in the first days, chicks cannot control their own body temperature. Temperature, ventilation, light, feed and water must follow the breed's management guide. Watch chick behaviour: huddling under heaters means too cold; panting and spreading to the walls means too hot.
  4. Growing: feeders and drinkers are raised as birds grow; feed changes from starter to grower to finisher; ventilation increases.
  5. Depletion: birds are caught and transported to the abattoir. Feed is withdrawn for a period before catching as the company specifies.

Layer production

Layer pullets are reared to point of lay with careful control of body weight and lighting, because lighting programmes control when hens start laying. During lay, hens need a steady light day, layer feed with enough calcium for strong shells, clean water and calm conditions. Eggs are collected several times a day, kept clean and cool, and graded.

Key production measures

MeasureMeaning
MortalityPercentage of birds that died
Average weightGrowth against the breed standard
Feed conversion ratio (FCR)Kilograms of feed per kilogram of live weight
Egg production percentageEggs laid per 100 hens per day
Egg weight and shell qualityGrading and price

lessons.title: Common poultry diseases
lessons.html:
Common poultry diseases

How disease spreads

Germs spread through sick or carrier birds, wild birds, rats and mice, flies and beetles, contaminated feed and water, people's clothes, boots and hands, vehicles, equipment and egg trays. Because thousands of birds live close together, disease can spread through a house in days.

Important diseases

  • Avian influenza (bird flu): highly pathogenic strains cause sudden high deaths, swollen heads, blue combs and wattles, drop in egg production. Spread by wild birds and contact. A controlled disease.
  • Newcastle disease: breathing problems, twisted necks, paralysis, green diarrhoea and deaths. Prevented by vaccination. A controlled disease.
  • Infectious bronchitis: coughing, sneezing, poor egg shells and drop in production.
  • Gumboro (infectious bursal disease): in young birds; weakens immunity so other diseases follow.
  • Coccidiosis: a parasite in the gut; bloody or watery droppings, poor growth; worse in wet litter.
  • Mycoplasma: chronic breathing problems, poor growth.
  • Salmonella: may cause disease in birds and food poisoning in people.

Reporting controlled diseases

Avian influenza and Newcastle disease are controlled under the Animal Diseases Act 35 of 1984. A sudden rise in deaths or signs of these diseases must be reported to the farm manager at once, who must notify the state veterinarian. Do not move birds, eggs, manure or equipment off the farm until instructed.

Signs of sickness

Watch for: birds sitting still with ruffled feathers, eyes closed, not eating or drinking, coughing or rattling breathing, abnormal droppings, swollen heads, lameness, a drop in feed or water use, or a sudden rise in deaths. Record and report.

lessons.title: Preventing and controlling disease
lessons.html:
Preventing and controlling disease

Biosecurity - the first line of defence

  • Isolation: fences, controlled entry, no other birds kept by workers where farm policy says so, wild birds kept out of houses.
  • Traffic control: visitors logged, vehicles disinfected, work from youngest to oldest birds.
  • Sanitation: shower-in or change, foot baths, hand sanitising, clean equipment.
  • All-in, all-out: each house is filled with birds of one age and emptied completely, then cleaned and disinfected before the next flock.
  • Pest control: rats, mice, flies and litter beetles controlled with baits and traps placed as the pest control plan requires.

Cleaning and disinfection between flocks

  1. Remove all litter and manure.
  2. Dry clean: brush and blow dust from walls, ceilings, fans.
  3. Wash with water and detergent.
  4. Disinfect with a registered disinfectant at the label concentration.
  5. Clean and disinfect water lines.
  6. Let the house dry and rest for the period the farm specifies.

Vaccination

Vaccines protect birds against diseases such as Newcastle disease, infectious bronchitis and Gumboro. They may be given at the hatchery, by drinking water, spray, eye drop, or injection, following the programme set by the vet. Keep vaccines cold, use them before expiry, and follow the method exactly. Water vaccines must not be mixed with chlorinated water unless a stabiliser is used as instructed.

Treatment

Treat only on the vet's advice, with registered products, at the right dose and for the full course. Observe withdrawal periods for meat and eggs, as stated on the label.

Dead birds

Collect dead birds daily, record numbers, and dispose of them by incineration, burial or the method the farm uses, away from the houses.

Key points

  • Brooding conditions must follow the breed's management guide and chick behaviour.
  • FCR measures feed used per kilogram of live weight.
  • Avian influenza and Newcastle disease are controlled; report suspicions at once.
  • Biosecurity, all-in all-out and pest control prevent disease.
  • Vaccinate and treat only as the vet directs, observing withdrawal periods.
